catalog_quote: Tone is phonemic in Navakat in that there are minimal pairs where the only distinguishing linguistic feature is the tonal distinction. Such pairs display a difference in intonation as well as in pitch, with the vowels with a low tone displaying a falling-rising tonal contour and the vowels with a high or neutral tone exhibiting a level tonal contour. ... làm 'path' lám 'shoe' ... Grammatical morphemes, such as the case markers and conjunctions, do not take tone. Exceptions are some grammatical morphemes in the verb complex: (-)sṍŋ [pst.vis], ʈò [probability], túk [inference]. The tonal distinction is predictable to a large extent. new_statements.quote: Tone is phonemic in Nàvakat in that there are minimal pairs where the only distinguishing linguistic feature is the tonal distinction. Such pairs display a difference in intonation as well as in pitch, with the vowels with a low tone displaying a falling-rising tonal contour and the vowels with a high or neutral tone exhibiting a level tonal contour. [...] At the same time, the tonal distinction is predictable to a large extent. [...] the main tonal distinction is found only in the first syllable, where plain nasals and liquids correlate with low tone, but nasals and liquids with preradicals correlate with high tone (Huang 1995; Zeisler 2004: 250–257). [...] The tone of the first vowel determines the tone of the following syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Navakat has an empty rule. Saxena 2011 supplies a word-prosody characterisation (first-syllable tone, Tibetan-type) but no stress statement, so it refines the empty record only by establishing the language as tonal with no stress claim; it neither agrees with nor contradicts any placement. Variety: the Nako village variety (Nàvakat), Upper Kinnaur.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Navakat (Nako village variety) is described as a tone language of the Tibetan type: a phonemic high/neutral vs low tone contrast carried by the first syllable, largely predictable from the initial consonant, with the first syllable's tone spreading to the following syllable. The paper says nothing about word stress, accent or prominence (the words 'stress', 'accent', 'prominence' do not occur anywhere in the text).
new_statements.exceptions: Tone is 'distinctly audible' in isolated words but 'not so distinct' in free speech, where the tonal contour is the main cue (p. 190); tonal contrast also marks transitivity in verb pairs (kòndʒa INTR vs kóndʒa TR, p. 190).
new_statements.identity_note: Saxena 2011 describes the variety of Nako village (Nàvakat, the villagers' own name is 'nau'), Hangrang sub-tahsil, Upper Kinnaur, Himachal Pradesh, and treats it as a Tibetan variety close to Tabo and Ladakhi. Sharma 1992 calls the same language 'Nyamkad (Nyam-kat)'; its chapter (pp. 97-196) also covers Spitian, Chhitkuli and Kanashi in the same volume, so if it is ever obtained the Nyamkad chapter, not the volume-level statements, is the relevant part.

sources.quote: No stress/accent statement anywhere in the article (a full-text search for stress/accent: stress/accent absent). Tone section is the 2011 original of the 2022 passage: 'Tone is phonemic in Nàvakat ... the main tonal distinction is found only in the first syllable ... The tone of the first vowel determines the tone of the following syllable.' plus one sentence dropped in 2022: 'While the tonal distinction is distinctly audible in lexical items when spoken in isolation, in free speech the tonal differences are not so distinct; instead the main distinctive feature is primarily the tonal contour.' (p. 190).

sources.quote: Part I covers only the Lahul languages (Pattani, Tinani, Gahri, Tod); the Nyamkad sketch is in Part 2 (1992), which is not online. Kept only because it shows Sharma's sketch template includes 'Supra-segmental phonemes' / 'Accent' subsections (e.g. Pattani 2.8.3, Gahri 2.6), so the 1992 Nyamkad sketch very likely contains an explicit accent statement.
